newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's U.N. envoy tipped to become foreign minister.
newsitem.headline: Iran's U.N. envoy tipped to become foreign minister.

text.p: Iran's ambassador to the United Nations, Kamal Kharrazi, emerged on Tuesday as frontrunner to become the Islamic republic's next foreign minister.
Two influential daily newspapers tipped the diplomat to take over from veteran Ali Akbar Velayati when President-elect Mohammad Khatami forms his first cabinet.
Khatami, a moderate Shi'ite Moslem clergyman elected by a landslide in May, is due to succeed President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani on August 3.
Iranian media have been speculating on the make-up of Khatami's cabinet, often giving different names for various portfolios, since the election.
All cabinet nominations have to be approved by parliament and the Guardian Council of senior clerics and lawyers, which has the final say.

The government-owned Iran Daily and Iran News, which often reflects the views of the Foreign Ministry, both named Kharrazi to succeed Velayati, the voice of Iran in foreign capitals since becoming foreign minister in 1981.
Velayati, a paediatrician by training, would become director of a Tehran hospital, one of the newspapers said.

Kharrazi, who like Velayati is in his early 50s, has been Iran's ambassador to the world body since 1990. After studies in Iran and the United States where he received a doctorate in management psychology, he held positions in Iranian state media and the Foreign Ministry.

He is on record as having said last November that no dialogue was possible then with the United States, Iran's arch-foe since militant students stormed the U.S. embassy in Tehran in 1979 after the Islamic revolution and held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days.
Washington severed ties with Tehran in 1980 after a failed U.S. military mission to free the hostages and relations have remained sour ever since.

U.S. President Bill Clinton in 1995 imposed trade and investment sanctions on Iran in an effort to isolate the country because of what Washington sees as Tehran's sponsorship of international "terrorism", attempts to acquire weapons of mass destruction and hostility to the Middle East peace process.
"Washington should first show goodwill and as a prerequisite must prove its readiness to abandon its hegemonistic and arrogant attitude," Kharrazi said in November.
Kharrazi's nomination for the Foreign Ministry was supposedly leaked to the press by an informed source, said the official news agency IRNA, which publishes Iran Daily.
Iran News said Velayati would become director of Masih-e Daneshvari hospital in northern Tehran.
